entries.content:
Chang Yang Jiao

Head of Blockchain, Nammu21

Moritz Platt

Capital Markets Technology Manager

The syndicated loan and private credit markets, both critical components of corporate finance, have long been constrained by manual processes, leading to multi-week settlements, valuation opacity, and trade friction.

To solve these long-standing challenges, fintech innovator Nammu21 partnered with Google Cloud on a new proof-of-concept. Using its AI-powered platform to structure legal agreements and instantiate them as smart contracts on the Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), Nammu21 automates the entire loan lifecycle, paving the way for improved settlement times and greater market efficiency.

Digitizing the loan market

While loan markets provide billions in capital to businesses worldwide, their underlying infrastructure has not kept pace with the speed of digital finance. This landscape requires continuous coordination across facility agents, borrowers, and diverse lender syndicates, while also managing highly customized credit agreements with dynamic tranches and complex covenants.

In particular, relying on fragmented, manual interpretation of legal text often results in significant operational drag and data silos. According to the Loan Market Association, secondary market settlement times for par/near par loans in Q4 2024 still averaged 42 days, with a median of 27 days. These notoriously slow timelines tie up capital, increase counterparty risk, and create a heavy reconciliation burden for participants.

Nammu21 transforms bespoke credit documents into programmable assets at scale by rendering each facility's governing terms as a Digital Credit Instrument (DCI). The DCI maps every term — including conditions, consents, eligibility criteria, and operational mechanics that determine what is permitted under a facility — directly back to its originating legal provision. These elements are then expressed as executable behaviours against a loan's live state.

To instantiate these instruments, the proof-of-concept utilizes the secure, high-performance execution environment of GCUL, an institutional-grade, permissioned distributed ledger that helps automate complex financial workflows to deliver near-instant transaction finality and predictable costs without the volatility or security concerns of public blockchains.

A purpose-built stack for digital credit

Combined with Nammu21’s data intelligence, GCUL provides the foundational infrastructure for converting legal document logic into live, programmable contracts. Designed to handle the privacy, scale, and multi-party coordination required by institutional finance, GCUL provides a permissioned, high-performance distributed ledger that delivers deterministic, instant transaction finality for high-value financial settlements.

Programmable contracts on GCUL are written in 

gculpy
, GCUL's domain-optimized programming language. As a strict, statically-typed subset of Python, 
gculpy
is designed to be safe, readable, and auditable, making it ideal for processing complex financial logic.

For regulated financial institutions, 

gculpy
offers distinct operational advantages over other ledger programming models. The language simplifies development by removing the need for complex memory management or workarounds to meet highly restrictive call stack limits, allowing engineers to focus on the financial logic itself. 

GCUL also provides robust, built-in permissioning, requiring explicit user authorization before a contract can store data on their behalf. This solves the "unsolicited asset" problem — common on public networks — where unwanted tokens can be sent to an organization's wallet, creating compliance and accounting issues. With GCUL, institutions can maintain full control over which assets they interact with to support their high-value, highly regulated use cases.

Nammu21 serves a dual role in this architecture. First, the platform renders the DCI programmatically from the original legal agreement without manual document reading to establish the terms. Next, it derives 

gculpy
contracts that define the structure of the obligation and govern the loan on GCUL, using the DCI to supply the terms that determine what the loan documents permit, require and block.

Technical architecture: The loan lifecycle on GCUL

Nammu21’s loan implementation on GCUL demonstrates the value of creating a single, immutable source of truth. The proof-of-concept modeled a $1.945 billion Term Loan B — one segment of a broader multi-facility transaction — where the agent bank, borrower, transferor, and transferee all worked off a permissioned view of the same on-ledger rendering.

The lifecycle begins when an agent bank selects a specific credit agreement transformed by Nammu21. The platform instantly provides the structured terms from the document, which are used to instantiate a unique 

gculpy
contract on GCUL, establishing a verifiable, on-ledger digital twin of that specific loan facility.

Next, the agent bank initiates the onboarding of the borrower and lenders. This multilateral action requires that each participant review the request and then provide explicit consent by approving the onboarding invitation from their own interface. Once all parties are onboarded, the agent bank records an immutable hash of the loan's key terms on-ledger, attesting that the on-ledger data matches the canonical off-ledger records.

Subsequent lifecycle events, such as secondary market transfers or repayments, are also managed as multi-step, automated workflows governed by a consent-driven model. For example, a transfer of a loan position requires new lender, borrower, and agent bank consent before it can be executed atomically on the ledger. All payment flows, from interest payments to loan close-outs, settle directly on GCUL using tokenized commercial bank money, eliminating the need for external payment rails.

Transacting with familiar, regulated money on a programmable ledger provides an architecture purpose-built for institutional finance, grounded in three core pillars:

1. Compliance via gated execution: Nammu21’s 

gculpy
contracts instantiated with governing terms, validate every action against the terms transformed from the agreement before execution, mitigating potential covenant breaches or invalid transfers upfront while eliminating the risk of silent failures. 

2. Role-based privacy: GCUL enforces strict, role-based access, ensuring that trading strategies, positions, and sensitive loan data remain confidential and are visible only to the necessary counterparties in a transaction.

3. Settlement finality: Every on-ledger action completes near-instantly and anchors on canonical data derived from the original credit agreement, replacing provisional, reconciliation-heavy models with real-time, trusted verification.

The business impact of moving on-ledger

This proof-of-concept illustrates a structural shift in how credit markets can operate. When each facility's governing terms are rendered as a DCI and executed on GCUL, the operational mechanics of lending markets change fundamentally, rather than incrementally.

Values can be reconciled bilaterally, but governance logic cannot – and the market’s current friction stems directly from each party's independent interpretation of the rules. Resolving this issue on-ledger is what enables settlement times to compress, back-office overhead to shrink, and counterparty risk to be mitigated by design rather than by manual checking.

This same architecture can be applied wherever credit terms are bespoke and manually interpreted. By freeing up capital that would otherwise be trapped in lengthy settlement cycles, new liquidity is unlocked and a more dynamic and efficient secondary loan market can emerge.

The team would also like to thank Someera Khokhar, Jordan Shelley, and Saskia A. Aalders at Nammu21 and Googlers Ishan Singh, Kathryn Stavish, Tom Chudy, and Stathis Onasoglou for their contributions.

entries.content:
Christine Goglia

Agentic Transformation Lead, Google Cloud

Over the past few years, our Google Cloud Consulting team has partnered with many companies to introduce AI into their daily operations.

In that time, we’ve seen the focus shift from generative AI that answers questions to agentic systems that fully carry out the work. These agents can create multi-step plans and manage a project from start to finish.

While budget, compute, and tooling can help launch an agent program, enterprise adoption takes intentional culture work. People need to feel empowered enough to experiment with agents, and leaders need to show teams what agents mean for their roles.

Based on our work across these organizations, we’ve put together five practical lessons for guiding enterprises through an agentic shift.

1. Make workflows agent-executed, human-directed

Most enterprise workflows run like a relay race: one person completes a task, checks it, and hands it off to the next person, who then does the same. Layering an AI agent onto that model gives you a faster runner for one leg, but the handoffs may stall or slow down other work.

Redesigning your workflows can remove blockers like these in a few ways:

  • Strategic direction: Move from human-in-the-loop validation (where a person checks each step) to a human-in-the-lead model. Agents take on the work, and people set the direction and own the outcomes.

  • Parallel dependencies: One agent can handle every dependency at once instead of passing work through a multi-person queue. For example, an agent can check product availability, credit limits, and contract paperwork at the same time without waiting on each step to finish.

  • Manage by exception: Once the process is set up this way, the agent absorbs routine deterministic transactions, routing only ambiguous or high-judgment scenarios to human review. Cross-team stalls disappear, and your team stays in control.

2. Turn hesitation into ownership

In our experience, the biggest barrier to adoption is trust. Many employees worry about their value if an agent handles most of their day-to-day tasks. Others are concerned with who takes the blame if an agent makes a mistake. We encourage teams to treat agents the way they'd treat a junior team member:

  • Active delegation: Frame agents as digital coworkers. That means assigning tasks to them, defining their scope, and checking their work for accuracy.

  • Clear responsibilities: Set boundaries around which decisions an agent can make and which require human sign-off. When team members know exactly where accountability sits, they can better direct agents.

  • Comfort through exposure: Confidence grows through familiarity. We recommend starting with low-stakes use cases (like scheduling internal meetings) to help motivate teams before moving to high-stakes operations (such as financial forecasting).

3. Manage hybrid teams of people and agents

Next, it’s important to support collaboration when you bring agents into your team. Let’s look at how this might work in practice,

  • Focus on results: Collaborate across teams to break down workflows at both the tool and task level. Cross-functional perspectives reveal an end-to-end view of the process, helping you pinpoint where agentic capabilities belong and how to prioritize ideas by technical feasibility and business impact.

  • Reinforce behaviors: Top performers on a hybrid team are the people who guide their agents well. Reward team members for auditing an agent's reasoning and catching when its logic drifts from company goals.

  • Coach your teams: Show your teams how to work with agents so people can spend more time on creative work and decision-making.

4. Build agentic literacy through experimentation

Your teams need to understand how agents solve problems. People who know where an agent's logic breaks down (and why) can guide and judge its output.

  • Beyond the tool: Literacy covers both writing a good prompt and auditing the result. Agents choose the most likely path instead of following deterministic rules, so people need to know when to trust an agent's output and when to check it.

  • Safe learning zones: Give business roles the same sandbox access that technical teams get to build agentic literacy across the whole organization.

  • Celebrating intelligent failure: Experimentation is how teams learn. In our experience, we’ve seen that when teams build an agent that fails because the data wasn't accurate, that team then understands how important data readiness is. Even if it didn’t work out, this should still be encouraged so your teams keep experimenting.

5. Govern agents with a hub-and-spoke model

To roll agents out across an enterprise, you need central guardrails that don't slow down the teams closest to the work. A hub-and-spoke model does both: it gives teams a shared foundation to build on and room to move at their own pace.

  • The hub: Establish a central AI council team that sets guidelines, maintains ethical guardrails, and manages a library of approved tools. That way, teams don't rebuild the same things.

  • The spokes: Allow individual teams to adapt those tools to their own needs, experiment quickly, and give feedback on what works in practice.

Within Google Cloud Consulting, we use our internal Agent Catalog to share low-code agents and skills that drive cross-team learning, innovation, and efficiency. However, you don’t need to build a custom platform to implement this. Here are a few approaches:

  • Filter and sort agents made by employees through a simple internal web app.

  • Publish and share agents with built-in Gemini Enterprise features like Agent Gallery.

  • Work directly with technical teams that help organizations create tailored solutions.

Lead with a people-first approach to AI

Becoming an agentic organization is about your people. Give your teams systems and guardrails to move fast, room to experiment, and leadership that promotes accountability.

Ultimately, the overarching goal is to build an organization where human ingenuity and agents support and amplify one another.

Get started

  • Explore free courses on Google Skills: Build in-demand AI expertise at your own pace and guide your teams through the agentic journey.

  • Join a Build with Gemini workshop: Sign up today to discover hands-on strategies for creating agentic literacy and empowering your teams to lead with AI.

entries.content:
Karl Weinmeister

Director, Developer Relations

Alan Blount

Product Manager

You’re probably hearing more about SKILL.md files, and you’ll see that a lot of people test them the same way: paste a prompt into chat, watch it pass once on a laptop, and merge to main. But when you paste three pages of CLI docs into a markdown file without an evaluation loop, you are just as likely to confuse a frontier model as you are to help it.

For the past weeks, we have been diligently measuring and optimizing our own Google Cloud Developer Plugin, with the most essential skills and the Developer Knowledge MCP server to ground responses in the documentation.

We ran dozens of scenarios with Gemini, Antigravity, and other agents. We used Claude Sonnet 5 on Gemini platform inside isolated Harbor pods on GKE Autopilot. And, we contributed Kubernetes and Gemini platform capabilities upstream to NVIDIA's open-source evaluator. 

Here's the five-rule engineering playbook we use to verify a skill is worth its tokens.

1. Gate trigger collisions and security risks before spinning up containers

When an evaluation run shows zero improvement between your plugin arm and your baseline arm (Δ = 0), the natural urge is to rewrite the body of your SKILL.md instructions. Hold off on that. Nine times out of ten, the agent never loaded your skill in the first place.

Coding agents do not read full SKILL.md bodies at turn zero. The router only inspects the short name and description in your YAML frontmatter. Once a workspace grows past a dozen skills, two failure modes collide: under-triggering (your description describes internal implementation rather than developer intent) and sibling hijacking (a broad phrase like "helps with cloud deployments" in a neighboring skill intercepts the prompt first).

We recently open-sourced skill-reach so you can catch frontmatter collisions before spending on container sandboxes. It validates manifests, computes vocabulary overlap against nearest rival skills, and runs empirical routing probes across Claude Code, Google Antigravity, and OpenAI Codex:

Pair skill-reach with NVIDIA's SkillSpector (Tier 1 and Tier 2 of SkillEvaluator). As the Nemotron Labs team details in their Evaluating Agent Skills deep dive, standard code linters miss agent-native risks buried in markdown prose: prompt injection, silent data exfiltration, tool poisoning, and trigger abuse. 

2. Never trust an eval that runs on a developer laptop

If you run skill benchmarks directly on your workstation, your numbers are lying to you. A developer laptop is packed with ambient state that contaminates the baseline arm:

  • Cached Google Cloud credentials

  • Exported project variables and warm bash history

  • Global environment rules

An unassisted baseline agent can pass a cloud deployment test by inheriting a default project ID or token sitting in your local shell profile, masking the exact failure your skill was written to solve.

Host resource contention also warps agent trajectories. While hill climbing code-retrieval agents with AlphaEvolve, our internal testing showed that running the exact same agent benchmark while a workstation was under CPU load dropped the score. Slower file scans and subprocess timeouts cause the agent to abandon search paths prematurely.

3. Measure paired WITH vs. W/OUT ablation (Pass@3), not vibes

Running prompts a single time and screenshotting the green checkmarks is not a real evaluation. Multi-turn tool-using agents branch on every shell exit code and stdout snippet. In our retrieval study, more than a third of benchmark tasks produced different scores across consecutive runs of the exact same code and prompt.

A perfect score is equally meaningless without a paired baseline for comparison. Both Claude's plugin eval tool and NVIDIA's SkillEvaluator run paired ablation across multiple repetitions: Arm A runs the base model in a clean sandbox without the skill, while Arm B runs the identical prompt and sandbox with the skill mounted.

Comparing the score improvements across our sandbox trials exposed three clear patterns that single-shot testing hides. Without the plugin, the base model still stumbled into a working deployment on most runs, but only after burning minutes of wall-clock time guessing deprecated flags and retrying bad requests. Conversely, when a test case shows identical success with zero efficiency gain, the base model already owns that capability natively. Your skill is pure context tax — delete it.

4. Separate efficiency and security from correctness so agents can't reward-hack

When you connect an evaluation harness to an automated optimizer (like AlphaEvolve or reach optimize), it is a surprisingly common pattern for the agent to cheat the grader.

In our AlphaEvolve retrieval experiments, evolved candidates discovered four distinct ways to game the benchmark without solving the task. When the grading harness blocked specific expected substring checks in source code, an evolved candidate dynamically concatenated strings at runtime, traversed up the directory tree, and read the ground-truth answer file directly off disk. Another candidate spawned subprocesses to bypass AST checks.

The evolutionary loop favored those cheaters because the fitness formula blended correctness (0.95 weight) and token efficiency (0.05 weight) into a single score. Reading the answer file from disk takes no LLM turns, earning an efficiency bonus that gives cheaters a survival advantage over honest agents that spent tokens searching the repository.

Hardening your skill evaluator against reward-hacking takes three structural guardrails. First, configure Harbor so your test fixtures, grading scripts, and answer keys live inside a dedicated verifier container that mounts workspace artifacts only after the agent container exits. Second, keep SkillEvaluator's five dimensions (Correctness, Discoverability, Efficiency, Effectiveness, and Security) strictly orthogonal; never let token thrift compensate for a failed test or a security violation. Third, in NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator#140, we extended security checks to fail any trial that reads Kubernetes service account tokens or queries cloud metadata endpoints, while redacting live OAuth tokens from saved trajectories.

5. Encode operational habits, not documentation dumps

Looking across all of our trials, the difference between the skills that delivered a score improvement in our sandbox benchmark and the community skills that failed came down to what was inside the markdown.

Skills that copy-paste public API reference tables into skill files yield almost no lift. Frontier models already have public cloud docs in their pretraining weights; dumping thousands of words of static flags into the prompt just inflates time-to-first-token and buries actionable constraints.

The skills that increased our Efficiency score in our test suite taught compact operational habits and verification reflexes instead of encyclopedic reference text:

  • Verify CLI flags at the leaf subcommand before mutating state: Rather than listing dozens of flags in markdown, the skill teaches a simple reflex: verify help output at the command line before executing a state-changing deployment.

  • Route through a lightweight catalog index on demand: Rather than loading fourteen heavy cloud skills into context at once, a thin root router checks a curated remote index and pulls only the specific recipe needed for the task.

  • Enforce least-privilege auth defaults: Explicit guardrails instruct agents to authenticate via Application Default Credentials rather than downloading static service-account JSON keys, while enforcing unauthenticated access restrictions alongside explicit invoker IAM bindings.

Because our evaluation stack runs in CI, upgrading models takes one flag change. We re-run the paired WITH vs. W/OUT matrix against the new model and delete every skill whose Delta drops to zero. Deleting a skill because the new model graduated past it is one of the cleanest high-fives in software engineering.

Get started

Ready to equip your coding agents with production-grade skills? Try the Google Cloud Developer Plugin for AI Coding Agents.

entries.content:
Google AI & Infrastructure

Authors: Burak Gokturk, VP Research & Development; Rujun Han, Research Scientist; George Lee, Product Manager.

Today, the Google AI & Infrastructure team is announcing Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE), a new benchmark and open competition, developed in collaboration with Mercor, and built to test a frontier model’s ability to complete tasks in mechanical, electrical, civil and structural engineering. 

To help the research community measure and improve how agents handle physical engineering work, we are releasing 29 public tasks, their grading tools, and an open competition leaderboard at ple-bench.com.

Frontier labs and the broader research community use model examinations to test AI’s progress in completing tasks in a specific discipline. Humanity's Last Exam measures a model’s general knowledge. Agents' Last Exam measures a model’s ability to complete digital professional work. Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE) measures a model’s ability to complete work that helps build the physical world. Physical engineers design skyscrapers, power grids, and computer chips we rely on, yet we could find no existing benchmark that tests whether frontier models can do that work end to end.

Why textbook benchmarks fall short for physical engineering

Frontier language models now score above 90% on many academic benchmarks. However, those benchmarks mostly test textbook-style questions, single tool calls, or small, self-contained design problems. For AI developers and researchers building agents for physical  engineering, existing benchmarks do not show whether an agent can produce safe, code-compliant, and cost-effective designs under a licensed engineer's review and control. As the demand for infrastructure development outpaces financing, there is a growing opportunity for agents to support engineers working to close this gap.   

Inside PLE: Real-world tasks built with practicing engineers

PLE closes this evaluation gap with 85 long-horizon tasks across four core disciplines: mechanical (30 tasks), electrical (27 tasks), civil (18 tasks), and structural (10 tasks) engineering.

Instead of answering a single prompt, an agent works inside a containerized project folder — built on Mercor’s Archipelago environment — that mirrors what a practicing engineer receives on the job. Each task holds an average of 61 files (5,170 total files across the benchmark), including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, 2D CAD drawings, 3D BIM models, and document revisions. The agent must reason through these files, find the governing building codes and physical limits, run calculations, and generate production-ready deliverables that a licensed reviewer would review and approve.

In collaboration with experts from Mercor and licensed practicing engineers from industry, we built PLE using two methods:

  • Expert-authored tasks (44 tasks): Practicing engineers created the project folders, prompts, and grading rubrics based on real professional engineering tasks.

  • Co-authored tasks (41 tasks): Practicing engineers designed the initial task and an agent pipeline assembled the task's environment and grader from licensable engineering standards. Engineers then validated and increased the difficulty of every task assembled by the agent.

All frontier models score below 50%

We tested 14 frontier models on PLE using seven publicly available agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenHands, and Pi). Because PLE evaluates both code compliance and cost efficiency, agents only earn points if their design passes every hard safety check first. Our baseline results show a wide gap between current models and real-world engineering requirements:

  • High headroom: All frontier models score below 50% on our private test set, with the highest-performing model on its native harness reaching a mean score of 48.3%.

  • Hard safety gates: While the top-scoring agent configuration satisfied 91% of individual constraints on co-authored tasks, only 41.3% of its deliverables passed every hard safety and feasibility check required.

  • Model vs. harness impact: Choice of model drives performance far more than the harness (up to a 50-point spread across models, versus a median 3-point spread across harnesses for the same model), though harnesses significantly affect run cost.

Test your agent and join the open competition

Evaluating AI agents on realistic project files, strict safety rules, and material costs is a practical step toward building helpful tools for physical engineers. Here is how you can get started with PLE today:

  • Check out the full technical breakdown in our PLE paper on arXiv.

  • Download the 29 public tasks, grading scripts, and evaluation container from our GitHub repository.

  • Bring your own agent setup and submit it for evaluation on our private test set at ple-bench.com—with 13 Google-sponsored models running free on our servers and prize details coming soon.

Building cloud solutions with autonomous AI agents should feel fast, safe, and reliable. Without cloud-specific context, coding agents often struggle. They might invent deprecated SDK syntax, guess invalid command flags, or attempt operations without the required Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. Even worse, an unguided agent can enable billable APIs or provision cloud resources without your explicit permission.

entries.content:
Nithin Tomson

Database Engineer

Adi Shtatfeld

Senior Product Manager

When database engineers hear “database migration", they typically think of a one-time onboarding pathway—moving databases from on-premises environments to the cloud, or between different cloud providers.

However, Google Cloud's Database Migration Service (DMS) supports Cloud SQL for SQL Server as a source. This opens up powerful, non-traditional operational patterns for SQL Server customers within Google Cloud. Because DMS enables continuous, low-downtime database replication between Cloud SQL instances—whether in the same project, across different projects, or across regions—it can serve as an everyday utility for day-two operations like storage management.

In this post, we explore a compelling operational use case for DMS with Cloud SQL for SQL Server: executing disk shrinks with minimal application downtime.

Why should I shrink my disk?

In many production environments, database storage only moves in one direction: up. Features like Cloud SQL automatic storage increase are essential for preventing out-of-space outages during unexpected traffic spikes, large batch imports, index maintenance, or temporary staging loads. Similarly, over the lifecycle of an application, you might archive historical records, purge obsolete data, or drop unused indexes.

When data is deleted, SQL Server marks the freed space inside your data files (.mdf, .ndf) as reusable for future writes; similarly, log truncation frees up space within transaction log files (.ldf). However, the database files themselves continue to hold their peak used space unless AUTO_SHRINK is configured — a setting that is generally not recommended in production due to severe index fragmentation and performance overhead.

With a manual shrink operation on the database files using DBCC SHRINKFILE, you can release that unused space from SQL Server files back to the underlying disk. Even after shrinking the database files, though, the Cloud SQL persistent disk remains at its peak allocated capacity. If you do not expect your database to grow back into that allocated disk space anytime soon, you should consider shrinking the disk itself to reduce ongoing storage costs — especially in scenarios such as:

After major data archiving or purging: You have permanently moved historical data to cold storage or BigQuery and your active dataset is now a fraction of its peak size.

Recovering from one-time storage spikes: A runaway transaction, large data migration, or temporary staging load triggered storage auto-increase, leaving you paying for terabytes of provisioned disk capacity you no longer need.

Post-refactoring or schema optimization: You have split tables out of a monolithic database into separate services, dropped large unused indexes, or applied data compression.

The query below allows you to inspect both the allocated capacity and available free space for each database file fo a database:

You can monitor the following key Cloud SQL metrics in Cloud Monitoring to identify whether your provisioned disk quota significantly exceeds actual disk usage, indicating an opportunity for disk shrinking:

  • database/disk/bytes_used
    : Tracks the actual amount of disk space currently consumed by your database files and logs. 

  • database/disk/quota
    : Represents the total provisioned disk capacity allocated to your instance.

Cloud SQL provides a built-in storage shrink feature to reclaim this unallocated disk space, which works well when your workload can tolerate a planned maintenance window. However, native disk shrinking requires instance downtime proportional to the total allocated disk size — which can mean hours of offline maintenance for multi-terabyte drives.

If your production SLAs cannot accommodate extended downtime, Database Migration Service (DMS) offers a minimal-downtime alternative. By continuously replicating your databases to a newly provisioned Cloud SQL instance with a smaller, right-sized disk, you can reclaim unused storage while your application stays online — requiring only a brief cutover window. To understand why this approach keeps your cutover window so short, let's first look at how DMS replicates data between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances under the hood.

How DMS works under the hood: Replication between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances

To leverage DMS effectively, it helps to understand its underlying replication mechanism. When migrating between Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances, DMS coordinates a synchronization process similar to native SQL Server log shipping.

  • Initial full backup: It captures an initial full backup (.bak) of the selected user databases and restores them on the target instance.

  • Continuous log backups: It continuously captures and applies transaction log backups (.trn) to keep the target instance synchronized in near-real time.

Because synchronization occurs at the user database level, objects residing outside of it—such as logins, linked servers, and SQL Server Agent jobs—are not automatically replicated to the standby instance. Consequently, server-level objects must be migrated manually.

Disk shrinking with minimal downtime

Using this continuous replication pipeline, you can reclaim unallocated storage without taking a lengthy maintenance window. Instead of shrinking the existing disk in place while the instance is offline, you migrate your workload to a newly provisioned Cloud SQL instance with a right-sized disk while your production application remains online.

The DMS disk shrink workflow

  • Provision a new target instance with a smaller, appropriately sized disk (leaving sufficient headroom for transaction logs and future data growth).

  • Start a continuous DMS job using your existing Cloud SQL instance as the source.

  • Let replication catch up while your production application runs uninterrupted.

  • Perform a brief cutover: Stop application traffic, let the final transaction log apply, promote the target instance in DMS, and repoint your application.

Comparison: Native shrink vs. DMS migration

As shown in the comparison above, because DMS migrates your workload to a new instance at the user-database level, a smooth cutover requires migrating your server-level objects and user mappings alongside your data. Let's look at the essential pre- and post-cutover steps to include in your runbook.

Pre and post-cutover essentials: Going beyond database replication

Pre-cutover preparation: Migrating server-level objects

Because DMS operates at the user-database level, server-level objects are not automatically replicated. You will need to create them manually in the destination instance before the cutover.

  • Script out logins from the source using 

    sp_help_revlogin
    and recreate them on the target instance.

  • SQL Server Agent jobs & Server-Level objects: Because DMS replicates databases rather than server instance state, objects outside user databases must be scripted from the source and deployed to the destination Cloud SQL instance. In SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), connect to your source instance, navigate to the object in Object Explorer, right-click and select 

    Script [Object] as > CREATE To > New Query Window / File
    :
    • SQL Server Agent jobs (
      SQL Server Agent > Jobs
      ): Inspect generated scripts to ensure job steps do not reference on-premises file paths or unsupported OS dependencies.
    • Linked servers (
      Server Objects > Linked Servers
      ): Follow the exact same scripting approach. Ensure you enable the 
      cloudsql.linked_servers
      database flag on your Cloud SQL instance before deploying.
    • Extended events (
      Management > Extended Events > Sessions
      ): Follow the same scripting approach. 

  • For TDE enabled instances, you will need to export the TDE certificate from source and import the TDE certificate to destination before. 

  • Instance Configurations (such as database flags, Active Directory, Entra ID configurations etc): These must be manually configured on the destination instance to exactly match the source settings.

  • If using Polybase you will need to re-encrypt DMK for the database-scoped credentials to function correctly.

Post-cutover remediation: Resolving orphaned database users

Database users mapped to SQL Server logins that are either absent or misconfigured on a server instance are unable to authenticate. These are termed orphaned users. Because logins created on the destination instance will possess unique Security Identifiers (SIDs) that do not match the source SIDs preserved in your migrated databases, users will be orphaned by default. Addressing this requires manual re-mapping once the target database is brought online following the cutover.

  • Detecting & re-mapping orphaned users: While using sp_help_revlogin preserves SIDs during login migration, creating logins on the destination instance via alternative methods generates new server-level SIDs. Because these differ from the source SIDs retained in the DMS-restored user databases, database users become orphaned after cutover and require re-mapping.

ALTER USER
): For each unlinked database user returned by the query, execute the following statement inside the context of that database to cleanly re-map the principal and its permissions to the new Cloud SQL server login:

Summary and next steps

DMS is more than a one-time bridge from on-premises environments into Google Cloud — it is a versatile tool for day-two operations in the Cloud SQL engineer's toolkit. When strict production SLAs prevent you from taking lengthy maintenance windows for a native disk shrink, DMS provides a reliable, managed replication pipeline to right-size your storage footprint and reduce infrastructure costs with minimal downtime.

To get started with configuring Cloud SQL for SQL Server as a DMS source, explore the official documentation. And if you're new to running SQL Server on Google Cloud, check out the Cloud SQL for SQL Server introduction.

entries.content:
Andrea Morange

Editor, Google Cloud

Editor’s note: Want to keep up with the latest from Google Cloud? Check back here for a monthly recap of our latest updates, announcements, resources, events, learning opportunities, and more.

This October, we took massive leaps forward in delivering flexible, open, and powerful enterprise AI solutions. From bringing Gemini 4 Argon to Google Cloud to expanding choice and flexibility, we’re giving organizations the tools they need to bring complex, multi-agent AI workflows into production safely.

Here’s a quick look at the major milestones, expert insights, and practical developer guides to read through and save.

Top announcements

  • Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems: We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

  • Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud: We announced the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

  • Google Cloud expands model choice and flexibility, bringing OpenAI models to customers: Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed source LLMs, alongside more than 200 first-party, third-party, and open models on a unified enterprise AI platform. 

  • Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity: In keeping with Google Cloud's commitment to an open ecosystem and to give developers the right model for every job, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity for Google Cloud customers. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for complex work while Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement.

  • Introducing Gemini for government services: Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all. 

  • Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 is now available on Google Cloud: For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Thought leadership (editor’s pick)

  • A new gear: How startups are advancing robotics with Google AI: We marked a major milestone in physical AI with the launch of Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2) on the Gemini platform and AI Studio, bringing Google DeepMind’s frontier multimodal reasoning and long-horizon task planning for robotics to Google Cloud. Read more from Darren Mowry, VP of Global Startups and Investor Ecosystem at Google, about the exciting work these startups are undertaking. 

News you can use

  • Developer’s guide to implementing MCP apps in Gemini: Enterprise assistants still respond mostly in text. However, that can break down for visual, multi-step work, where every adjustment costs another slow chat turn. This guide takes you through implementation in Gemini. 

  • Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins: Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds. 

  • Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators: In this post, we explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality. 

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

September

This September, we brought you new how-to guides, model updates, and security innovations to help you find-and-fix. From Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar to Mantis, there’s no shortage of new ways to apply AI to your work.

Notably, we announced Gemini 4 Argon, our next era of frontier intelligence. Gemini 4 Argon delivers frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense. You can learn more here. 

Top announcements

  • Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar is now generally available: Following our announcement of Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar is now generally available in Gemini Enterprise.

  • Getting started with Mantis, our open-source bug finding-and-fixing harness: Available to all as an open-source framework, Mantis is part of Google’s internal approach to find and fix vulnerabilities at machine-speed. It creates a more effective scalable, context-aware repository analysis. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick)

  • Racers, start your agents: Formula E brings realtime AI to the edge: Chasing records at the Goodwood Hillclimb, Formula E used Gemini Enterprise, Gemma, and a Pixel phone bolted to the dash to push the envelope of AI and edge computing.

News you can use

Best practices guide for customizing Gemini models via Reinforcement Learning (RL): In this guide, we will walk through practical best practices for using RL fine-tuning service. We'll start with a short tour of the RL training loop, how to decide if and when to use RL, and introduce how to get the most value from this approach.

Empower your agents with the Google Cloud CLI remote MCP server: Powered by the popular gcloud and bq (BigQuery) command-line tools, this new server gives AI agents immediate, broad access to command-line operations for managing Google Cloud infrastructure and working with advanced BigQuery workflows securely and seamlessly. 

Graph Workflows in ADK: Everything you need to know: Using a refund workflow in ADK, we'll cover fan-out and fan-in, deterministic and agent routers, human-in-the-loop pauses, parallel workers, and dynamic orchestration— along with when to use a static graph or let Python decide what runs next.

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

August

This month, we focused on making AI highly practical for your business, including its associated costs. This meant tailoring our models for specialized industries – starting with Financial Services and Legal – and helping you keep your budgets under control. Let’s dive in!

Top announcements

  • FinOps for the AI era: New flexible billing and cost controls for agents: To help you get better return on AI, we announced expanded billing flexibility and new cost management tools for agent workloads across Gemini Enterprise and developer tools like Google Antigravity in Gemini Enterprise and Android Studio. 

  • Gemini Enterprise for Financial Services: We’re bringing Google’s agentic AI directly into the workflows of capital markets and corporate banking.

  • Gemini Enterprise for Legal: Gemini Enterprise for Legal provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across firms and corporate legal departments. 

  • Expanding Google Antigravity for enterprise customers: Antigravity is available now as part of eligible Gemini Enterprise app subscriptions, including out-of-the-box administrative and spend controls.

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

  • Tokenomics: Why smart teams spend more on AI, on purpose: Hear from Eric Lam, Head of Value, Delta, Google Cloud Consulting about how disciplined organizations are moving past reactive sticker shock over AI bills and embracing tokenomics. 

  • Meet the researcher fighting AI hallucinations at Google Cloud: Cyrus is a senior research scientist at Google. Lately, his focus has shifted to large language models, specifically a persistent issue known as hallucination, which is when an artificial intelligence model lacks the correct facts but confidently invents an answer anyway.

  • What sports cars can teach us about optimizing AI spend: More tokens doesn't always mean better AI. Read our conversation with Mike Clark, Director of Product Management for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, on how to balance horsepower with efficiency and get the highest return out of every dollar you spend on AI.

News you can use:

Looking for a steer on your foundation or inspiration for your next project? Take a look at some of our favorite how-to guides from August:

  • 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype: These ten are scoped to the prototype-to-production transition itself. Each question ends with a short, runnable snippet you can copy into your own project today. Adjacent decisions that matter just as much but aren't specific to that move, your data layer and RAG architecture, CI/CD, network design, are deliberately out of frame here.

  • Your chance to start building AI agents from the absolute basics: Agent Valley is a free, 5-week live learning series designed to take you from scratch to building your very own hands-on agent systems. And instead of staring at boring terminal lines, you’ll be building and playing inside a tiny, low-poly virtual world!

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

July

Since launching the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform a few months ago, we’ve watched businesses move from basic experiments to serious, production-grade builds. We want to make it even easier — and more secure — for you to scale those systems.

Along with a batch of new platform updates, this month we’ve put together 13 practical demos and 20 diagnostic questions to help your engineering teams align on a strong architectural blueprint. Let’s dive in!

Top announcements

  • What’s new in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: In this helpful recap, we announced some of our most popular capabilities are available for everyone, from Agent Runtime to Agent Identity.

  • Now in preview: Find and fix software vulnerabilities with CodeMender: As adversarial AI threats accelerate attacks on code, security teams must counter them with machine-speed defenses that can automate code remediation and fight AI with AI. You can learn more about CodeMender and review the documentation here.

  • Solve harder problems with AlphaEvolve, now available to everyone on Google Cloud: AlphaEvolve is a code optimization and discovery agent built on top of Gemini that helps solve the hardest algorithmic problems and achieve breakthroughs for your business and research. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

If automation requires delegation, then delegation requires trust. But letting an AI agent run on its own is a big leap for any business. While the productivity gains are clear, the fear of losing control is very real. This month, we sat down with our experts to discuss how leaders can navigate this shift by focusing on transparency, predictability, and setting clear boundaries for how agents handle weird data exceptions.

Here’s our picks for the month to learn more.

  • How leaders can scale AI by trading control for trust (Q&A): We sat down with Michael Gerstenhaber, VP of Product Management for Gemini Enterprise, to discuss why the future of AI is about defining safe boundaries.

  • What makes an AI agent trustworthy: Context is fast becoming one of the most valuable assets a company owns. Prajakta Damle, Senior Director, Product Management, shares what it takes to get trustworthy AI right. 

News you can use:

What if you’re looking for a steer on your basic foundation, inspiration for recipes, or some inspiration? Take a look at some of our favorite how-to guides from July:

  • Automate your agent development lifecycle using any coding agent: Stuck prototyping? With Agents CLI skills, you can go through the different phases of the entire agent lifecycle without ever leaving your coding agent.

  • Why AI apps fail in production (And how Google solved it): Only 5% of AI prototypes make it to production, and the other 95% fall into the validation abyss. How can you move confidently into production? 

  • 13 hands-on demos to build on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Not sure where to start with Agent Platform? Here’s 13 ways you can stir up some creativity. 

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

June

Our main focus in June was helping your teams build, scale, and secure AI. Today, we’re sharing a fresh roundup of updates designed to help you run smarter, more secure applications while keeping everything under your control.

We even shared a cool virtual shopping demo at Cannes to show how retailers can make product discovery more exciting. Let’s dive in!

Top announcements

  • Introducing the Open Knowledge Format: We introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that formalizes the LLM-wiki pattern into a portable, interoperable format. This is a vendor-neutral, agent- and human-friendly standard for representing the metadata, context, and curated knowledge that modern AI systems need.

  • Collaboration with Apple on its expanded Private Cloud Compute (PCC) systems: Our collaboration with Apple is built on a foundation of deep commitment to privacy that leverages Google Cloud's security and privacy technologies. At the heart of this collaboration is our Confidential Computing portfolio and our Titanium security architecture.

  • Claude Fable 5: Available on Google Cloud: Claude Fable 5, Anthropic’s latest frontier model, is now generally available on Google Cloud. This launch is the latest proof point of our ongoing commitment to bring the industry's latest models straight to our Agent Platform. 

  • Cloud Atelier: How Gemini Enterprise is helping restyle the retail playbook: This year at Cannes, we showcased Cloud Atelier — a destination-based, virtual shopping experience that highlights how retail brands can turn this classic dilemma into an exciting moment of product discovery. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

  • How Google Cloud Security uses AI internally: To counter machine-speed, AI-driven threats, we’ve worked hard to transition Google Cloud’s security posture to an autonomous, proactive model. By embedding specialized AI agents directly into our software development lifecycle (SDLC), we’ve created automated guardrails that protect code at a scale and speed unreachable by human teams — and we’re taking steps to make those same guardrails widely available.

  • The 4 lessons that guided AI Threat Defense: We introduced Chris Betz as the new CISO of Google Cloud. For his first Cloud CISO Perspectives, Chris shares four key lessons we learned about using AI to the defender’s advantage while building AI Threat Defense.

News you can use:

  • 5 lessons from red teaming AI applications: To help you build AI securely, Mandiant has developed a proactive, risk-based approach centered on the Good AI Assessment (GAIA) Top 10, outlined in our new report, Secure Development of Generative AI Applications: A Proactive Approach. 

  • How to unlock true ROI in software development – a deep dive into the latest DORA research: To help you evaluate the costs and business benefits of AI, we recently shared the DORA: ROI of AI-assisted software development report. This research offers a practical approach to help your team work through early adoption challenges, align engineering plans, and drive business growth.

  • Agent Factory Recap: 100X engineering with AI agents in Google Antigravity 2.0: In this episode of the Agent Factory, Shir Meir Lador, Head of AI Engineering, Google Cloud Developer Relations, sat down with Rody Davis, one of Google’s top agentic engineers. They dive into the massive shift from traditional IDEs to agent-first platforms, the reality of code reviews in an AI-driven world, and how to use "skills" to perform at a 100X level.

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

May

We’ve had a busy month! Between announcing Gemini Spark and Gemini 3.5 at Google I/O – and unveiling Google AI Threat Defense, our latest AI-powered cybersecurity solution, we had a lot to share with Google Cloud customers. Keeping up with the latest news takes time, so we gathered the most important announcements, thought leadership, and technical guides in one place to help you quickly catch up.

To learn more about our I/O announcements, here’s everything you need to know for Google Cloud customers, and top news for startups.

Top announcements

Introducing Google AI Threat Defense to help you outpace the adversary: Google Cloud is introducing a comprehensive AI-powered cybersecurity solution — Google AI Threat Defense — an always-on autonomous security platform. Learn more here.

  • Gemini 3.5: Our latest family of models combines frontier intelligence with action – starting with Gemini 3.5 Flash.

  • Gemini Omni: Our new model is a leap forward in world understanding, multimodality, and editing, letting you generate any output from any input, starting with video.

  • Google Antigravity: Google Antigravity’s expanded capabilities and new integration with Agent Platform bring agentic development to your entire organization.

  • Gemini Spark: For Gemini Enterprise and Workspace customers, Gemini Spark is your 24/7 personal AI agent that helps you work more efficiently by autonomously taking action on your behalf, under your direction.

  • Google Workspace: Google Pics, our new image generation and editing tool, and new voice features in Gmail, Docs and Keep, help reimagine how you work.

  • Managed Agents API on Agent Platform: Allows developers to build and run custom agents inside secure, Google-hosted environments that seamlessly integrate with Agent Platform.

  • CodeMender: A powerful AI security agent provided through Agent Platform, CodeMender can help find and fix vulnerabilities in your code.

Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro are generally available: Available today via Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, organizations are already putting the models to work. Learn more here. 

Thought leadership (editor’s pick):

  • Cloud CISO Perspectives: How Google + Wiz changes multicloud strategy for CISOs: Vinod D’Souza, director, Office of the CISO, shares highlights from his RSA Conference fireside chat with Anthony Belfiore, chief strategy officer, Wiz. While threat actors have seen gains from the adversarial misuse of AI, Google and Wiz are tackling these challenges head-on by combining Wiz's deep cloud telemetry with Google's world-class AI and quantum research to help CISOs and their organizations meet the needs of the agentic enterprise era. Read more here.

News you can use:

What Google I/O '26 means for developing agents on Google Cloud: Dig deep into how Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and the new developer tools shared at I/O fit together, unpack the spectrum of choice for building, and share what we’d actually try first. Learn more here.

  • Five must-have guides to move agents into production with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Here is a look back at our five-part series covering the architecture patterns and best practices you need to move your agents into production. Learn more here.

  • How to build an AI-ready security program for the public sector: From industrial control systems to decades-old municipal databases, here’s our CISO guidance to prep AI-ready security programs for the public sector. Learn more here.

Stay tuned for monthly updates on Google Cloud’s AI announcements, news, and best practices. For a deeper dive into the latest from Google Cloud customers, read our monthly recap, Cool stuff customers built.

April

We hosted Google Cloud Next in Las Vegas on April 22, announcing incredible innovations from Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to our eight-generation TPUs. We also expanded the Gemini Enterprise app in collaborative ways – now, with new features like Projects, you can work side-by-side with your agents and colleagues. 

If you missed the livestream, take a look at our Day 1 recap. It’s been incredible to see how customers have been applying AI in thousands of ways — so far, we’ve counted more than 1,300 examples. 

Top announcements

1. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Our new, comprehensive platform to build, scale, govern, and optimize agents. Moving forward, all Vertex AI services and roadmap evolutions will be delivered exclusively through the Agent Platform, rather than as a standalone service, to power the next generation of agent development.

The platform is designed around four core pillars — build, scale, govern, and optimize — that allow teams to collaborate seamlessly. Learn more about Agent Platform here.

2. Gemini Enterprise app has all the key components to let teams discover, create, share, and run AI agents in a single environment. At Next ‘26, we introduced several new capabilities in the Gemini Enterprise app:

  • Agent Designer uses the same no-code agent designer experience of Agent Platform and lets employees build sophisticated schedule- and trigger-based agents using any enterprise connector. It gives you a virtual flowchart of your agent, allowing you to inspect, test, and approve workflows, ensuring total transparency for executing critical business processes.

  • Long-running agents are designed to execute complex business processes. They can work autonomously in secure cloud sandboxes, giving agents the ability to orchestrate business logic, write code to build custom tools, and complete multi-step work like reconciliation activities or sales prospect sequencing — without needing constant prompting.

  • Inbox in Gemini Enterprise provides a central location to monitor, guide, and help manage all of your agent activity, including your long-running agents. Notifications are intuitively categorized into actionable groups like "Needs your input," "Errors," and "Completed.”

  • Projects create a dedicated space where the agent’s memory is confined to the files and conversations your team adds. By connecting it to data sources including Google Drive, NotebookLM, and Google Group Chats, the agent becomes an expert on a specific topic and can provide team members daily briefings or status updates without digging through months of documents.

  • Skills create simple shortcuts using an “@” mention for repetitive tasks such as applying brand guidelines, formatting a report, and accessing specific data.

  • Canvas gives our customers an interactive editor directly within Gemini Enterprise. It allows teams to easily create and edit Docs and Slides, and even export to Microsoft 365 files, within the same experience.

  • Agent Gallery provides access to third-party agents from partners like Adobe, Atlassian, Lovable, and ServiceNow, and is adding more third-party connectors for Asana, Mailchimp, Workday, and more. These integrations enable your agents to retrieve data and execute tasks with your systems-of-record. 

3. AI Hypercomputer: Designed specifically for demanding AI workloads, our AI Hypercomputer is an advanced, purpose-built architecture that unites performance-optimized hardware for compute, storage, networking, open software and machine learning frameworks — as well as flexible consumption models — into a single, integrated system. We are announcing innovations at every layer of the AI Hypercomputer:

  • TPU 8t, optimized for training, uses breakthrough Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) technology to scale up to 9,600 TPUs and 2 PB of shared, high-bandwidth memory in a single superpod. It achieves 3x the processing power of Ironwood and delivers up to 2x more performance/Watt.
  • TPU 8i, optimized for inference, uses our new Boardfly topology to directly connect 1,152 TPUs in a single pod. It features 3x more on-chip SRAM compared to previous versions to host larger KV caches entirely on-silicon and integrates a specialized Collectives Acceleration Engine. Taken together, TPU 8i delivers 80% better performance per dollar for inference than the prior generation, enabling millions of concurrent agents to run cost-effectively.

4. The Agentic Data Cloud: A new data architecture built for the speed and scale of agentic AI. The Agentic Data Cloud delivers an AI-native architecture, allowing agents to perceive, reason, and act on your behalf in real-time, including:

  • Cross-Cloud Lakehouse, standardized on Apache Iceberg, is our Lakehouse that enables you to leave your data in AWS or Azure (coming later this year) while querying it instantly — without the friction of vendor lock-in or the cost of data movement

  • Knowledge Catalog constructs a unified, dynamic context graph of your entire business enabling you to ground agents in all of your business data and semantics. With Smart Storage and the Object Context API, files in Google Cloud Storage are instantly tagged and enriched with metadata before an agent touches them. Then our Knowledge Engine uses Gemini to autonomously tag, define logic and instantly map complex relationships across your entire enterprise, providing the semantic definition your agents have been missing.

5. Protecting the agentic enterprise: Security built for the AI era. Our full-stack AI approach, from the chips to the models, gives you a competitive advantage with better integration and velocity to help protect customers. Not only can Google action insights from the world’s largest threat observatory and Mandiant frontline experts, but we also bring cutting-edge insights and breakthroughs from Google DeepMind, to help make your platforms more secure.

  • Agentic defense: Three new agents in Google Security Operations can help hunt threats, engineer detections, and provide context on third parties. You can build your own security agents with remote Google Cloud model context protocol (MCP) server support for Google Security Operations, now generally available. You can also access the MCP server client directly from the Google Security Operations chat interface, available in preview.
  • Protecting AI and cloud apps across any infrastructure with Wiz: Newly expanded AI coverage helps build secure agents across clouds and AI studios. New AI-Bill of Materials in development tools can help secure AI-generated code and mitigate the risk of shadow AI. Learn more.
  • Securing agents and the agentic web: Model Armor can integrate with Agent Gateway, and new Agent Identities provide more layers of defense against shadow AI. Google Cloud Fraud Defense, the next evolution of reCAPTCHA, offers agent-specific capabilities that can help secure the agentic web as well as the entire user and customer journey.   
  • Trusted Cloud: We’re simplifying permissions with modern IAM, and advancing Google Cloud security with new capabilities in Security Command Center plus new innovations in data and network security.
